blocks.text: The separation is not a rule I invented: the agent kit's own index marks the chats an agent started for another chat, and the terminal's own picker hides exactly the same ones. The switch on the chat bar brings them back and is remembered between visits.

content.label: What you see now
content.lead: The list is names you recognise; opening one shows the conversation.

shots.caption: Real names, the folder each ran in as its own colour, two tickets and a count, and no Resume button
An opened chat: the state, the model, three tickets and “+21”, and what was said in it before

blocks.text: The lines the harness writes into a chat's record — the notifications it posts to an agent, the echo of a typed command — are left out, because nobody said them. Six chats I opened while testing were read in before that rule existed, so those six still show them; every chat opened from now on is clean.

decisions.title: A chat an agent started is hidden, not deleted
decisions.why: Your words were that they should be filtered with a way to enable them. They are still there, one press away, because a review agent's chat is sometimes exactly what you want to read.

decisions.title: A chat's past is read in once, and only the words
decisions.why: The record is the agent kit's, not ours, and reading it twice would say everything twice. Tool calls are left out: a past chat's tools cannot be re-run and a row saying one ran tells you nothing you can act on.

decisions.title: The last 200 messages, and the rest as a line
decisions.why: Those records reach 1002 messages. Drawing every one of them is the fault that made this screen take ten seconds in the first place.

decisions.title: The click is the consent
decisions.why: Nothing in the list wakes an agent by itself, which is the rule that stops a screenful of chats becoming a bill. Clicking a chat's name is a deliberate act, so it can carry the waking too — and the row says “waking” while it does.

next.if_nothing: The job sits waiting on your look; nothing else moves on it.
